newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn stresses support for Transrapid rail project.
newsitem.headline: Bonn stresses support for Transrapid rail project.

text.p: The German government on Thursday stressed its support for the Transrapid high-speed rail project despite increasingly shrill political opposition and signs that private-sector backers are reviewing their commitments.
Opposition Greens deputy Gila Altmann said the final cost of the planned Hamburg-Berlin route would be far higher than official estimates, and passenger traffic far lower, making fares unaffordable.
In a parliamentary debate called by her party, she urged Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann to "admit what we have all known for a long time, that Transrapid is a dinosaur doomed to extinction".

But Wissmann said the multi-billion mark magnetic levitation train, which would link Germany's two largest cities in under an hour at a top speed of 420 km/h (260 mph) is just the kind of high-tech project needed to create jobs in the next century.
"We need the Transrapid, because it will open export opportunities for new, high-level technologies from our country," Wissmann told parliament.
His was echoed by Dirk Fischer, a Christian Democrat (CDU) deputy, who said, "The government, and the coalition parties in parliament, want this project, stand behind the project."
German media have been portraying the demise of the Transrapid as a foregone conclusion.
"Its fall is certain," the weekly Die Zeit said in a commentary on Thursday. "It is not enough that a technology functions well. It must also find its place in the world."

Press reports cited by Altmann have said a study due by April of the expected costs and revenues of the project will show that fares need to be 0.60 marks per passenger-kilometre, double earlier projections.
Wissmann rejected that assertion as "simply untrue", and urged deputies to await the results of the study.

Elke Ferner of the opposition Social Democrats said the Transrapid development funds would be better spent on improving existing rail technologies like the ICE, which has been a disappointment in export markets.

Construction is due to start in 1998, and operations begin in 2005. The government has said it will cover the costs of the Hamburg-Berlin track, while the private-sector partners develop and operate the train.
The private partners are led by Thyssen AG, and include Siemens AG, ADtranz, Hochtief AG, Philipp Holzmann AG, Bilfinger & Berger Bau AG and Deutsche Bahn AG.
Thyssen Chairman Dieter Vogel said that in the current environment of tight budgets, the anti-technology doubting Thomases could gain the upper hand.

"I cannot exclude (the possiblity) that one of the few future technologies Germany now has to offer could disappear in a drawer," he told Die Woche. "Without a political go-ahead, we will be very careful with further investments in Transrapid."
An administration spokesman on Wednesday told parliament the government viewed the current debate as a attempt by the partners to position themselves for coming contract talks.

Ottfried Hennig, head of the CDU in Schleswig Holstein, called on Thyssen to make a binding commitment to the project now, or withdraw. Siemens could replace Thyssen as leader, he said in a radio interview.
Thyssen seemed to be trying to put pressure on the government so that it could increase its profits. "This is not Chicago, this is the social market economy," he said.
